title: Global arable land redistribution toward the tropics and drylands under human settlement expansion
source: Scientific community and society : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: Arable land extent has undergone widespread changes across many regions worldwide through processes such as urban encroachment, forest conversion to agriculture, and dryland farming expansion. Yet an integrated understanding of global arable land dynamics remains limited. Using our self-developed arable land product integrated with global human settlement layers, Köppen–Geiger climate classifications, and historical land-use reconstructions, we show that the disproportionate climatic co-location of arable land and human settlements fundamentally structures global arable land dynamics. Across much of the climatically favorable Northern Hemisphere, earlier co-development of settlements and agriculture has increasingly shifted toward competition, with settlement expansion displacing cultivation from temperate regions and contributing to its expansion into adjacent arid zones. In contrast, low-latitude tropical regions continue to expand both systems at the expense of natural landscapes, partly driven by agricultural investment from Northern Hemisphere. Globally, these contrasting trajectories reveal a broader redistribution of agricultural pressure from climatically favorable regions toward less-exploited tropical and arid environments, linking settlement expansion and agricultural displacement to diverse environmental consequences including deforestation, biodiversity loss, groundwater depletion, and vegetation greening. These findings highlight the need to consider both local settlement–agriculture competition and broader agricultural redistribution when planning future food production and settlement growth.

title: Direct atomic-scale observation reveals rare earth element fractionation at mineral–water interfaces
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
abstract: Clay minerals, ubiquitous across diverse geological systems, exert fundamental controls on critical geochemical processes, particularly through their adsorptive interactions with economically vital elements such as heavy rare earth elements (HREEs). The adsorption of HREEs onto clay surfaces is not only the key process that enriches these critical resources but also a potential archive for dating significant weathering events. However, the atomic-scale mechanisms governing the preferential adsorption and fractionation of rare earth elements (REEs) at mineral–water interfaces have remained poorly constrained. Here, employing in situ atomic-scale imaging via high-resolution atomic force microscopy, we systematically investigate the adsorption behaviors of light and heavy REEs (La, Y, Yb) onto key crystallographic planes—Si-basal, Al-basal, and edge terminations—of representative clay minerals (kaolinite, illite, mica) under environmentally relevant conditions (pH 4.8 to 6.4). We directly visualize and quantitatively reveal that Si-basal planes selectively enrich HREEs with pH-enhanced adsorption capacity, whereas Al-basal planes exhibit negligible REE adsorption below pH 5.8 but preferential HREE adsorption at pH 6.4. Integrating synchrotron X-ray absorption spectroscopy, we identify the adsorption mechanism of REE on Si-basal and Al-basal/edge planes as outer-sphere complexation and inner-sphere binding, respectively. Furthermore, we quantify the contributions of distinct planes via surface complexation modeling, revealing Si-dominated to Al- and edge-controlled adsorption with elevating pH. These atomic-scale findings not only resolve long-standing debates about clay mineral-mediated REE fractionation but also redefine fundamental paradigms of surface reactivity at silicate mineral–water interfaces, offering insights into the cycling and metallogeny of other critical metals in aqueous and sedimentary environments.

title: The efficiency of information gain by natural selection
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
abstract: Natural selection enriches populations for genotypes that are well adapted to their environments, accumulating information about the selective conditions in the process. Therefore, selection can be viewed as a learning process through which populations acquire information about the environment. Motoo Kimura derived a relationship between the amount of information gained by selection and a measure of the inefficiency of the selective process, known as substitution load [M. Kimura, Genet. Res. 2, 127–140 (1961)]. Due to the gradual nature of selection and the ongoing mismatch of types to the environment, a lineage that is still acquiring information has lower mean fitness than a lineage that already has it. While this has been an influential insight, we find that Kimura’s model is inconsistent with selection experiments involving Escherichia coli . To address limitations in this model and develop a more robust measure for the efficiency of selection, we turn to computational learning theory. We show that the learning-theoretic concept of regret quantifies the inefficiency of selection as a learning process in terms of relative lineage fitness. We establish bounds on the efficiency of information gain in general settings, including frequency-dependent selection and arbitrary environmental change. We experimentally validate these bounds and demonstrate that our extended theory recovers Kimura’s fundamental insight. Finally, we show that selection is an asymptotically optimal algorithm for the basic problem faced by evolving populations and that it acquires information more efficiently than comparable processes in complex environments.

title: A chemomechanical bifurcation landscape unifies sustained growth, length homeostasis, and regenerative collapse in axons
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
abstract: Axonal growth machinery is largely shared across neurons, but axons exhibit strikingly different fates depending on developmental and environmental context: sustained elongation in peripheral neurons under permissive conditions, length homeostasis in cortical neurons after target innervation, and pathological collapse into dystrophic endbulbs in injured adult central nervous system (CNS) axons. These divergent outcomes have resisted explanation by length-sensing and biomechanical models that treat long-range transport and local force generation as separate problems. We unify these phenomena through a mechanochemical model that couples bidirectional motor transport and intracellular signaling to growth-cone balance of axonal tension, actomyosin contraction, and adhesion within a single feedback loop: The lengthening axon uses its own growing transport delay to establish self-limiting mechanical feedback, as the accumulating delay reshapes signaling waveforms to progressively elevate myosin contractility against actin-driven protrusion. Two physical parameters, the transport delay and the signaling feedback strength, organize axon fate into a unified state-space landscape spanning sustained growth, length homeostasis, and pathological collapse. Reduced feedback strength weakens this self-limiting mechanical feedback by simultaneously enhancing protrusion and suppressing contractility, providing a mechanistic interpretation of axon lengthening under partial reduction of retrograde transport. Bistability in the inhibitory regime explains why mature CNS tracts persist where nascent sprouts collapse, recasting regenerative failure as a state-dependent gate rather than a capacity limit. The framework predicts that partial rather than complete inhibition of retrograde transport could shift collapsed axons across the bifurcation into a growth-permissive regime, identifying a class of interventions complementary to existing capacity-restoration strategies for nerve injury.

title: A sulfotyrosine motif in the human TrkB extracellular domain is required for activation by the agonist antibody ZEB85
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
abstract: The brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF)-tropomyosin receptor kinase B (TrkB) signaling axis is a key effector of synaptic plasticity and neuroprotection. While TrkB activation is a major target to prevent neural dysfunction, stimulation with exogenous BDNF administration has not proven tractable given the unfavorable physiochemical properties of BDNF. In addition, BDNF also activates a cell death pathway by binding to the neurotrophin receptor p75. The TrkB agonist antibody ZEB85 provides an alternative route to the selective activation of TrkB. To understand the ZEB85 mechanism of action, we mapped the binding site for ZEB85 to the TrkB extracellular juxtamembrane domain and found a sulfotyrosine modification at residue 400 crucial for ZEB85 interaction and activation of TrkB signaling. We determined the structures of ZEB85 and BDNF bound to their respective binding sites on human TrkB suggesting independent sites for each ligand, despite prior evidence of direct competition. Using structure-guided BDNF- and ZEB85-binding deficient TrkB mutants, we assessed their ability to sequester ligands from full-length TrkB in cultured human neurons. We found that the BDNF binding site extends into the juxtamembrane domain of TrkB but does not require the sulfotyrosine 400 to activate TrkB. Together with biophysical analysis and AlphaFold modeling, these results explain how BDNF can displace ZEB85 from TrkB through an overlapping epitope. Our findings reveal unique features of TrkB, not present in the related neurotrophin receptors TrkA and TrkC and suggest future directions to explore the role of sulfotyrosine in TrkB signaling.

title: Elucidating molecular regulatory rules of nanoparticle biological identity via standardized deep proteomics
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
abstract: The biological identity of nanoparticles is often redefined upon exposure to physiological fluids through the formation of a protein corona (PC), However, the molecular rules linking synthetic design to biological fate remain elusive owing to the fragmented and inconsistent proteomics data. Here, leveraging a standardized deep proteomic database of 42 diverse nanomaterials, we reveal the general molecular selection rules that govern the PC formation. We demonstrate that the PC is not a product of random adsorption but is shaped by strict property-dependent recruitment. First, surface charge regulates cellular uptake, with anionic nanoparticles specifically recruiting adhesion proteins to promote Itgav-mediated endocytosis, thus forming a causal charge-corona-receptor chain. Second, PEGylation engineers immune evasion by selectively depleting specific complement and coagulation factors, rather than merely preventing protein adsorption. Third, nanoparticle geometry imposes structural constraints and selects proteins based on specific physicochemical features such as lysine content. Beyond mechanistic insights, we show that material-specific PCs can rebalance the serum proteome and enable the detection of low-abundance disease biomarkers. This work shifts the paradigm from empirical description toward rule-based prediction and provides a foundational framework for rationally engineering nanomedicines with predictable and programmable biological identities.

title: Complexity functions of infinite sequences
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
abstract: We address the inverse problem for complexity functions of infinite words, which asks which functions can occur as complexity functions of infinite words. We survey our recent advances on this problem and several of its ramifications. We describe an asymptotic solution to the inverse problem, realizing every function satisfying two necessary conditions as the complexity function of an infinite word up to asymptotic equivalence. We then turn to phenomena beyond asymptotic equivalence, presenting constructions of infinite words with seemingly contradictory behavior of the discrete derivatives of their complexity functions. These lead to a solution of a 1995 problem of Cassaigne and to applications in symbolic dynamics, including the question of convergence of Rauzy graphs, as well as to the growth and asymptotic invariants of algebraic structures.

title: Global bee bioregions mirror those of other taxa despite a uniquely bimodal latitudinal diversity gradient
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
abstract: Bioregionalization, the partitioning of the globe into areas of biotic similarity, is one of nature’s most striking patterns, and highly congruent boundaries have been identified across plants, tetrapods, ants, and butterflies. However, these taxa also share a unimodal latitudinal diversity gradient (LDG), raising the question of whether bioregionalization and the LDG are mechanistically coupled or instead arise from largely independent processes acting on different timescales. Bees (Hymenoptera: Anthophila) provide a natural test, their diversity peaking at mid-latitudes rather than in the tropics. Using range estimates for 3,370 species and a phylogenetic beta-diversity framework, we recover 21 bee bioregions nested within at least six major realms (Australasia, Indomalaya-Oceania, Nearctic, Neotropics, Palearctic, and Sub-Sahara) that closely align with those of other taxa despite bees’ atypical diversity gradient. We propose that bioregionalization and species richness are decoupled because they arise from distinct processes: the former reflects historical dispersal and evolutionary history, the latter local diversification, extinction, and environmental filtering. Our analysis provides a global biogeographic framework for future bee research and highlights the processes shaping the world‘s major biogeographic boundaries.

title: Intrinsic function of leptin receptor–regulated endothelial PD-L1
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
abstract: Programmed cell death ligand-1 (PD-L1) is an immune checkpoint protein expressed in vascular endothelial cells (ECs). In contrast to cancer, our understanding of endothelial PD-L1 in relation to metabolic syndromes and its vascular complications is less studied. For example, its regulation and intrinsic function remain unclear. Here, we showed that endothelial PD-L1 is regulated by leptin receptor signaling in male mice. In particular, endothelial PD-L1 expression is affected by leptin resistance. A lack of leptin receptors leads to PD-L1 downregulation in vascular ECs via posttranslational degradation. To understand the fundamental roles of endothelial PD-L1, RNA interference and selective knockout are employed in human endothelium and animals, respectively. Silencing or deleting endothelial PD-L1 expression delays cell cycle progression and proliferation due to rat sarcoma (RAS)/mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) inactivation. In obesity, endothelial PD-L1 deficiency impairs the EC turnover and worsens the vascular function. Overall, we provide an insight into how endothelial PD-L1 contributes to vascular homeostasis, suggesting its pathophysiological importance in maintaining cellular turnover.

title: Secondary organic aerosol formation from sequential oxidation of toluene and cresols
source: Earth and environmental sciences : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: Cresols are important urban emissions that can form multiple oxygen containing condensable vapors when they react with OH radicals in the atmosphere. These molecules contribute to secondary organic aerosols that have strong implications on climate and human health. In this work, we present flow reactor oxidation experiments demonstrating the rapid (sub-second) formation of condensable vapors with up to 10 oxygen atoms from the three cresol isomers (ortho-, para- and meta-cresol) under atmospheric conditions. Our quantum chemical calculations reveal that initial OH additions to the hydroxyl containing carbon atom lead to geminal diol intermediates that are critical to the rapid formation of condensable vapors from cresols and their key oxidation product, 3-methylcatechol. Incorporating these autoxidation mechanisms into model simulations shows that they contribute significantly to secondary organic aerosol composition. These results could explain the strong multi-generational contributions to aerosol from toluene and cresol, enabling a more accurate assessment of their climate and health impacts.

title: Hydration at the base of the mantle transition zone by ancient subductions in Asia
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
abstract: Whether and how the subduction processes result in water enrichment at the base of the mantle transition zone (MTZ) remain elusive. The major orogenic belts of the Asian continent, including the Central Asian, Tethyan, and Alpine–Himalayan belts, which record extensive subduction processes, offer an ideal target to address the hydration of the MTZ and its relationship with subduction. Here, we map water content at the MTZ base by combining mineral physics constraints on hydrous pyrolite and global seismic observations of velocity structure and 660-km discontinuity topography. Our results indicate an average global water content of approximately 0.14 wt%, with pronounced hydration anomalies in parts of Asia. Linking these anomalies with reconstructions of past subduction events since 410 Ma reveals extensive water delivery to the MTZ, particularly beneath parts of the Mongol–Okhotsk suture zone, the Central Asian Orogenic Belt, and the Tethyan orogenic domain, where water content exceeds 0.5 wt%. These results connect ancient subduction history to present-day mantle hydration, offering insights into Earth’s deep water cycle.

title: Computation and sampling for Schubert specializations
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
abstract: We study a problem at the interface of enumerative algebraic geometry, algebraic combinatorics, and the statistical mechanics of vertex models with long-range interactions. We develop methods to explore the values S w ( 1 , … , 1 ) of Schubert polynomials (called principal specializations), which count reduced bumpless pipe dreams (RBPDs) with boundary permutation w ∈ S n . We exhibit counterexamples to the conjecture of Merzon and Smirnov that S w ( 1 n ) is maximized on layered permutations; the smallest such example we find is at n = 17. Despite the counterexamples, we present bounds that support a refined conjecture that the maximum of S w ( 1 n ) over all w ∈ S n grows at the same asymptotic rate as the maximum over layered permutations (found by Morales, Pak, and Panova). We implement and benchmark four recurrences for Schubert specializations: the descent formula of Macdonald, the transition formula of Lascoux–Schützenberger, the cotransition formula of Knutson, and the formula of Billey, Jockusch, and Stanley. We also explore typical random permutations drawn with probability proportional to S w ( 1 n ) , equivalently from uniformly random RBPDs. Our simulations reveal a permuton-like limit analogous to the Grothendieck setting studied by Morales, Panova, Petrov, and Yeliussizov. For sampling, we show that the standard monotone Coupling From The Past framework does not apply to RBPDs, leaving exact uniform sampling open. To bypass this, we develop an efficient Markov chain Monte Carlo sampler augmented with macroscopic “droop” updates that preserve connectivity and accelerate mixing. Our publicly available fast implementations reach n = 20 for exact computation of S w ( 1 n ) and n = 100 for Markov chain Monte Carlo sampling using a chain whose stationary distribution is uniform on RBPDs (run on a cluster).

title: Crowding limits relative bacterial surface accumulation with density-induced effective heating
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
abstract: The accumulation of microswimmers near walls has been studied for decades. While hydrodynamics and single-cell kinematics are well-explored, the role of cell-cell interactions remains understudied. However, in realistic, crowded environments such as the human gut, these interactions can be just as crucial. Here, we demonstrate that they actively weaken bacterial surface accumulation. Analysis of entrapped cell tracks reveals that crowding enhances orientational fluctuations, which increase the effective rotational diffusion and facilitate wall escape. A minimal model shows that this collective effect is equivalent to raising the system’s effective temperature with density.

title: The ABCD hypothesis
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
abstract: If α and β are cardinals, then the cardinal exponentiation α β is the set of all functions from α into β . The ABCD hypothesis is the statement that for all infinite cardinals α ≤ β and γ ≤ δ , | α β | ≤ | γ δ | if and only if α ≤ γ and β ≤ δ . The Axiom of Determinacy, AD, states that every two-player infinite game on ω has a winning strategy for one of the two players. Let Θ be the supremum of the ordinals onto which R surjects. This paper will show that if AD holds and V = L ( R ) , then the ABCD hypothesis holds below Θ .

title: A symbiogenic merger enabled by oxygen initiated the evolution of eukaryotes
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
abstract: Recently, extensive genetic information about archaeal hosts at the basis of eukaryogenesis has come to light. Characterization of these first eukaryotic common ancestor (FECA) related organisms allows improved understanding of the enigmatic FECA to last eukaryotic common ancestor (LECA) transition. However, these gene-centered discoveries have the unfortunate side effect of entrenching erroneous ideas about early eukaryotic evolution. This is apparent in the two-Domain vision of life, with eukaryotes seen as specialized Asgard archaea, while underestimating the contribution of the endosymbiont to eukaryogenesis. Establishment of the alpha-proteobacterium as the future mitochondrion is treated as one of many such endosymbiotic occurrences, ignoring its unique evolutionary position. I will marshal evidence for symbiogenic mechanisms involved in the FECA to LECA transition, with a key role for the endosymbiont’s electron transport chain and its acceptor molecular oxygen, especially in the incarnation of reactive oxygen species occurring in the host cytoplasm. We should overcome overestimating gene determinism, while not sufficiently allowing for effects of biological hierarchies, emergent properties, and chance. Many eukaryotic properties are best understood by envisaging the crucial uptake of the future mitochondrion as a merger instead of an acquisition. This merger is characterized by a new kind of elaborate cellular entity emerging as a result of rapid coevolution, replacing a scenario in which already complex pre-eukaryotes acquired endosymbionts, accompanied by important, but limited, changes. Successful mergers are rare because they are intrinsically more difficult, but synergistically open up completely new areas of possibilities, as illustrated by incredible eukaryotic success.

title: Ddx3x deficiency in mice impairs corticofugal motor circuits and causes motor deficits that are attenuated by early-life exercise
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
abstract: The X-linked RNA helicase DDX3X is a high-risk gene for autism spectrum disorder and intellectual disability primarily in females. Individuals with pathogenic variants in DDX3X have pervasive and often severe motor manifestations. Using mouse models, we studied the circuits underlying the motor phenotypes associated with Ddx3x deficiency and examined the feasibility of an early intervention to ameliorate motor trajectories. We show that Ddx3x controls both the development and later plasticity of motor circuits connecting the motor cortex with the pontine nuclei. Ddx3x haploinsufficiency during development affects the dendritic arborization of corticopontine neurons. Juvenile-onset Ddx3x loss in corticopontine neurons is sufficient to induce adult motor impairments overlapping with those caused by chemogenetic disruption of corticopontine circuits. Further, Ddx3x mutant mice engage corticopontine circuits in skilled motor tasks in a sex-dependent manner. Last, Ddx3x haploinsufficient female mice undergoing a juvenile motor intervention show long-lasting specific benefits in their adult motor function. Together, these findings establish Ddx3x as an essential regulator of corticopontine neuron development and function and provide an early motor intervention to ameliorate motor outcomes in a mouse model of DDX3X haploinsufficiency.

title: CryoET imaging reveals that mitotic spindles are locally organized by microtubule density and Eg5 activity
source: Biological sciences : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: When eukaryotic cells divide, a mitotic spindle, composed of microtubule filaments interacting with molecular motors, self-assembles and is responsible for aligning and segregating chromosomes to the opposite daughter cells. Recent structural studies revealed that spindles are composed of short microtubules that do not span the full pole-to-chromosome distance. It remains unclear how these short, disconnected microtubules collectively assemble a bipolar spindle. Using cryo-electron tomography to map microtubule polarity in human spindles, we find that microtubules organize with consistent 8 nm wall-to-wall spacing. Spacing scales inversely with local microtubule density, consistent with organization by density-driven steric interactions, analogous to liquid crystal ordering. We find that the Eg5 motor establishes local antiparallel overlap independently of spindle bipolarity, while a balance of Eg5 and dynein regulates microtubule density to maintain spindle architecture. Together, these findings reveal the mesoscale principles by which cells build complex, self-healing cellular architectures from nanoscale building blocks.

title: The accuracy-safety trade-off of large reasoning models in clinical diagnostics
source: Biological sciences : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: Large reasoning models (LRMs) offer potential advantages for clinical diagnosis over standard large language models (LLMs), yet their utility and safety remain unclear. Here we show, on AIMS-LDR, a long-context diagnostic reasoning benchmark built upon real-world electronic health records, covering six matched model pairs and 12 specialties, that LRMs generate over 34% more false positive diagnoses and show approximately 40% lower reproducibility than their LLM counterparts, while making more accurate primary diagnoses and more clinically relevant differentials. Experiments confirm this trade-off across prompt designs, model hyperparameters, and evaluation paradigms. A structured collaboration model, in which the LRM broadens diagnostic coverage and the clinician verifies reliability, increases diagnostic accuracy by 20% and reduces false positives by 44% in a 15-physician validation study. These results, obtained under controlled retrospective conditions, suggest that pairing LRM reasoning with physician oversight may support safer and more accurate diagnostic decision-making, warranting prospective validation before clinical deployment.

title: Deuteration of arenes in D2O exclusively driven by single-atom Pt sites under visible light
source: Physical sciences : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: Deuterated arenes play crucial roles in medicinal chemistry and materials science (e.g., psychotropic drugs and deuterated OLEDs). However, the desired late-stage deuteration via conventional hydrogen isotope exchange methods always demands expensive isotopic reagents (e.g., D2, C6D6, or C2H5OD), metal complex catalysts, or harsh conditions ( ≥ 120 oC, 20 bar H2). Here, we report a single-atom photocatalytic strategy for efficient deuteration of electron-rich arenes using D2O as the deuterium source. Under visible light irradiation at ambient temperature in an inert atmosphere, a single-atom photocatalyst (Pt1/TiO2) affords high deuterium incorporation across 54 electron-rich arene substrates. The protocol is mild, sustainable, and scalable: gram-scale synthesis of deuterated arenes (11.98 g, 100 mmol) was successfully realized. Mechanistic studies indicate that the catalytically active sites are primarily Pt–O coordinate bonds, whose light-modulated charge distribution facilitates a possible electrophilic platinization pathway for C–H activation before H/D exchange.

title: Tree shrew more closely recapitulates primate spermatogenesis than the mouse in cross-species single-cell transcriptomic analyses
source: Biological sciences : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: The rapid evolution of spermatogenesis limits the utility of mouse models for studying human spermatogenesis because some genes are absent or divergent in mice. Primate models face practical and ethical constraints, whereas tree shrews are closely related to primates and suitable for laboratory research. Here we integrate histology and single-nucleus RNA sequencing data from human, rhesus macaque, mouse and tree shrew testes to assess the tree shrew as a model of human spermatogenesis. We show that transcriptional landscapes in tree shrew spermatogenic cells, particularly late-stage spermatids, more closely resemble those of primates than mice. Conservation and enrichment analyses identify two core gene modules shared among humans, macaques and tree shrews but distinct in mice. Gene expression trajectories also align between tree shrews and primates, including for genes without murine orthologs. Immunostaining and RNA-FISH support representative expression patterns. These findings define contexts in which tree shrews can complement existing models of human spermatogenesis and male infertility.

title: Exaiptasia diaphana core microbiome members are lost under climate change conditions despite host thermal tolerance
source: Biological sciences : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: Acute and chronic exposure to elevated temperatures associated with Global Climate Change (GCC) threatens the structure and function of host-associated microbiomes, yet predicting microbial responses to heat stress remains challenging. We exposed two lines of the sea anemone, Exaiptasia diaphana, to acute and chronic thermal stress to quantify the impacts on cnidarian physiology and microbiome composition. Acute exposure caused rapid algal bleaching that was paired with pronounced shifts in bacteriome structure in both lines within 14 days of thermal exposure. Chronic exposure significantly affected the population structure, photo-physiology and bacteriome composition in only one host line, suggesting acclimation capacity depends on host-algal genetic backgrounds. Using 16S rRNA amplicon sequencing of 493 individuals sampled across 180 days, we found that sampling date explained nine-fold more variation in the microbiome composition than temperature exposure. Despite this temporal variation, we identified 16 indicator taxa that consistently changed in relative abundance under thermal stress. These taxa became central hubs in microbial association networks with increasing levels of thermal stress, suggesting they played key roles in bacteriome reorganization. As many of these taxa were present in other cnidarians, including reef-building corals, they may represent targets for conservation strategies that aim to enhance resilience on reefs.

title: Local albumin excess exacerbates Candida albicans-induced inflammasome activation linked with hyperinflammation during vulvovaginal candidiasis
source: Biological sciences : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: Vulvovaginal candidiasis (VVC) is a mucosal yeast infection, mostly caused by Candida albicans, where symptoms are driven by inflammation. The onset of VVC is instigated by C. albicans pathogenicity, but the underlying causes of disease-driving hyperinflammation remain incompletely resolved. We found that vaginal albumin concentrations are higher in women with recurrent VVC and during experimental VVC in mice. These albumin levels correlated with inflammatory cytokines in vaginal lavages. While the abundance of this serum protein in the vagina can be a hallmark of inflammation-induced vascular permeability, we reveal molecular mechanisms by which albumin can also drive inflammation. Albumin increased NLRP3 inflammasome activation in human macrophages elicited by C. albicans. This was associated with increased resistance of C. albicans to macrophage-mediated clearance in the presence of albumin. Further, albumin increased the expression of fungal secreted aspartic protease 1, which we identified as the effector driving inflammasome activation and IL-1β responses in vitro and in an in vivo VVC model. Moreover, neutrophils also exhibited impaired clearance of C. albicans in the presence of albumin. Collectively, vaginal albumin may not only be a consequence of inflammation of the vaginal mucosa, but also can drive C. albicans-induced hyperinflammatory IL-1β responses that underlie immunopathology in VVC.

title: Darutigenol ameliorates experimental colitis via promoting Akkermansia muciniphila-mediated proline synthesis
source: Biological sciences : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: The gut microbiota dysbiosis is a key factor leading to inflammatory bowel disease (IBD). Darutigenol (DL) is a natural compound with limited oral bioavailability but potent anti-inflammatory activity. However, its ameliorative efficacy in colitis and precise mechanism remain unexplored. This study demonstrated through multi-omics analysis and fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) experiments that the alleviation of colitis in male mice by DL is dependent on the gut microbiota. Mechanistically, DL specifically enriches the abundance of Akkermansia muciniphila (A. muciniphila), which alleviates colitis by promoting the synthesis of proline. Interestingly, DL was found to promote the growth of A. muciniphila in the gut by targeting indoleamine 2,3-dioxygenase 1 (IDO1). Additionally, exogenous proline supplementation alleviated murine colitis by downregulating the IL-17 signaling pathway and its downstream cascades. Our findings reveal that DL ameliorates colitis by inhibiting IDO1 expression to drive A. muciniphila expansion and proline synthesis, and highlights the potential of DL for the treatment of IBD.

title: Increasing prevalence and expanding diversity of tet(X4)-carrying Salmonella in China
source: Biological sciences : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: The plasmid-mediated tigecycline resistance gene tet(X4) threatens the efficacy of tigecycline. While prevalent in Escherichia coli across diverse ecological niches, its evolutionary trajectory in Salmonella remains underappreciated. Here, we conducted nationwide genomic surveillance of 42403 clinical nontyphoidal Salmonella isolates collected from diarrheal patients in China between 2014 and 2025, of which 102 were tet(X4)-positive. Although the overall prevalence remained low, detection showed a statistically significant upward trend over 2019-2025. Importantly, the newly accrued 2025 data were broadly consistent with short-term forecasts generated by the beta regression model, providing partial support for short-term trend consistency. Genomic analyses showed that tet(X4) remained concentrated in ST34 but was also detected in additional sequence types, including ST469, ST8971, ST11 and one isolate with an unassigned ST, across multiple provinces, indicating broader geographic representation and genetic diversification. Plasmid analyses likewise revealed broader replicon diversity, with the dominant IncHI1A/IncHI1B/IncFIA background accompanied by less frequent IncHI2/IncHI2A, IncI1(Alpha) and IncFIA/IncFIB/IncFIC. Phylogenetic analyses further revealed shared clustering of the dominant plasmid background across host species and bacterial genera, consistent with cross-host and cross-genus circulation.

title: Viral tRNA-like structure hijacks host ribosomes for poly(A)-independent translation
source: Biological sciences : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: Positive-sense RNA viruses often use 3′ tRNA-like structures (TLSs) instead of poly(A) tails to capture the host translation machinery. While TLSs resemble canonical tRNAs and engage host factors, their ability to directly recruit ribosomes has remained unresolved. Here, we present cryo-electron microscopy snapshots of the histidine-accepting TLS (TLSHis) from tobacco mosaic virus bound to the tobacco 60S subunit, the 80S ribosome, and the 80S-tRNAiMet initiation complex. Across these states, TLSHis is consistently anchored to the L1 stalk of 60S, even under cycloheximide treatment, yet remains dynamic on the 40S subunit. Structural analysis shows that TLSHis transitions from the E-site to an adjacent Z-site to accommodate initiator tRNA. Functional assays show that TLSHis preferentially associates with ribosomal subunits over polysomes and can substitute for a poly(A) tail to promote robust cap-dependent translation. These results provide structural and mechanistic evidence that the viral tRNA mimic exploits the tRNA-exit channel to stabilize initiation-competent ribosomes and drive poly(A)-independent translation.

title: Stabilization of insulin receptor mRNA by Star-PAP in metabolic homeostasis
source: Biological sciences : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: Conserved polyadenylation b3y poly(A) polymerases (PAPs) is essential for mRNA stability, yet its metabolic functions remain unclear. Here we identify a rare variant p.D469N (Asp469Asn) in Star-PAP present in lean individuals but absent in obese cases. Adipose-specific Star-PAP knockout mice develop progressive adipose tissue loss, hepatic steatosis, and severe insulin resistance, phenocopying human lipodystrophy. Mechanistically, Star-PAP directly binds the insulin receptor (InsR) mRNA 3’–UTR to stabilize its transcript. Both deletion of Star-PAP and p.D469N variant decrease InsR mRNA maturation. Star-PAP deficiency impairs insulin receptor signaling and adipocyte lipid storage, while restoring InsR in adipocytes partially ameliorates the lipodystrophic phenotypes. Notably, Star-PAP deficiency disrupts acetyl-CoA homeostasis secondary to insulin signaling defects, accompanied by reduced histone acetylation at fatty acid synthesis genes. Pyruvate supplementation effectively restores acetyl-CoA levels and histone acetylation, thereby rescuing the gene expression and lipogenesis. Together, our results identify Star-PAP-mediated RNA polyadenylation as a mechanism governing adipose mass, positioning Star-PAP as a key regulator of insulin receptor signaling and lipodystrophy.

title: Proximity labeling of the Listeria monocytogenes surface reveals pathogen control of a host deubiquitinase
source: Biological sciences : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: Listeria monocytogenes navigates a crowded intracellular environment by recruiting host factors to its surface in order to hijack the host actin cytoskeleton for motility and cell-to-cell spread. Although these types of Listeria-host interactions are critical for infection, systematic characterization of this interface has been limited. Here, we implement the biotin ligase split-TurboID to profile host proteins recruited to the surface of L. monocytogenes during intracellular infection. We show that the host deubiquitinase CYLD is enriched at the pathogen surface. While CYLD promotes infection by suppressing innate immunity in macrophages, how L. monocytogenes recruits and appropriates CYLD function in other cell types has remained unclear. We demonstrate that L. monocytogenes uses the secreted effector Internalin C (InlC) to redirect CYLD to M1-linked linear ubiquitin at the bacterial poles. Despite its localization, CYLD does not deubiquitinate bacteria or regulate autophagic clearance in epithelial cells. Instead, CYLD and InlC protect L. monocytogenes from IFN-γ- and RNF213-dependent restriction of cell-to-cell spread. Overall, our work profiling the bacterial surface-host interactome has identified a mechanism by which InlC spatially reprograms CYLD activity to promote cell-to-cell spread in epithelial cells. These findings highlight how L. monocytogenes exploits a host deubiquitinase to perform cell-type-specific functions during infection.

title: Antimicrobial peptides derived from Nemuri induce ribosomal condensation to inhibit translation
source: Biological sciences : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: Antibiotic resistance is a global health threat requiring antimicrobials with alternative modes of action. Growing evidence indicates that bacteria organize key intracellular processes through biomolecular condensates and other forms of spatial organization, yet whether such spatial organization can be exploited as an antimicrobial target remains unclear. Here, we identify intrinsically disordered antimicrobial peptides, generated from the Drosophila sleep-inducing protein Nemuri, that inhibit bacterial growth by targeting ribosomal organization. Mechanistically, these peptides enter bacterial cells without overt membrane disruption and accumulate in ribosome-rich regions, where they bind broadly to RNA and ribosomal surfaces through multivalent interactions. This engagement remodels ribosome-rich regions into condensates with reduced ribosomal mobility, thereby suppressing global protein synthesis and distinguishing these peptides from canonical site-specific ribosome-targeting antibiotics. Furthermore, Nemuri-derived peptides exhibit broad-spectrum antimicrobial activity, including activity against drug-resistant pathogens, with low cytotoxicity toward Drosophila and mammalian cells. Together, our findings identify the organization and material dynamics of bacterial ribosomes as a biophysical vulnerability that can be exploited by antimicrobial peptides, revealing how a naturally evolved metazoan host-defense system turns intracellular organization itself into an antibacterial target.

title: Widespread selection of antibiotic resistance within hospital sewers
source: Biological sciences : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: Environmental microbiomes are sources of diverse antibiotic resistance determinants that can be mobilized and transferred to human pathogens under a selection pressure from antibiotics. Hospital sewers contain more antibiotics than most environments and are thus increasingly recognised as potential arenas for resistance evolution. However, it is unknown if resistance selection occurs there and what the drivers are. Here we show selection of antibiotic-resistant bacteria within Swedish hospital sewers. Evidence include; consistent selection of multiple resistances in Escherichia coli exposed to filtered wastewater from ten hospitals, but not to corresponding municipal wastewaters; in-situ enrichment of resistant over sensitive E. coli from wastewater to sewer biofilms at hospitals, but not at municipal sites; and higher resistance in bacteria collected from hospital sewers than from municipal sites as assessed by culturing and metagenomics. Evidence for drivers includes complete rescue of sensitive E. coli by addition of resistance genes to fluoroquinolones and β-lactams, and cellular effects typical for β-lactams. Measured concentrations by liquid-chromatography-tandem-mass-spectrometry compared to selective thresholds identify ciprofloxacin and cefotaxime as principal selective agents. Antibiotic concentrations and use data allow extrapolation of risks beyond Sweden. Given the absence of detectable selection at municipal sites, mitigations of risks in hospital sewers should be prioritized.

title: Aberrant thymic architecture and enhanced interferon signaling in Down syndrome
source: Biological sciences : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: Individuals with Down syndrome (DS) have an elevated risk of autoimmune disease, particularly celiac disease, type 1 diabetes, and autoimmune hypothyroidism. In DS, thymi show characteristic structural and cellular changes, but the connection between these and the propensity to autoimmune disease is still unclear. Here we present a cell atlas from single cell RNA-sequencing (scRNA-seq) and spatial transcriptomics of age-matched thymi from infants with and without DS, which might contribute to filling this knowledge gap. DS does not significantly alter CD34+ diversity in the thymus; however, the gene expression changes we observe indicate altered differentiative potential in DS CD34+ cells. Although many genes involved in T-cell development and function (including USP16, RUNX1 and ETS2) are located on chromosome 21, several important T cell regulatory genes that are located on other chromosomes also change in DS. In contrast, CD34- DS thymocytes are characterised by maturation defects. CD34+ progenitors and proliferating DP thymocytes are in a functional state of chronic interferon activation. In summary, we identify several notable differences in key functional cellular subsets and pathways within the DS thymus, providing insights into the spatiotemporal dynamics of the thymic environment for this genetic condition.
